strengths: The paper delivers the first systematic parameterized complexity analysis of Satisfiability in Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, and the classification is essentially tight: positive results (FPT for SATprob_lin by d+tw, XP by tw, FPT for SATcounterfact_lin by d+n; Theorems 5 and 11) are paired with matching lower bounds under standard assumptions (Theorems 2, 7, 8, 9), giving a nearly complete map of the 3x3 expressivity matrix from the parameterized viewpoint.

The hardness results are established under remarkably strong restrictions, which strengthens them considerably: Theorem 1 shows NP-completeness of arbSAT with edgeless primal graphs and d=2, Theorem 2 shows ∃R-completeness even for n=1 or edgeless binary instances, and Theorem 9 shows NP-completeness of SATcausal_lin even when all edges of the primal graph are pairwise vertex-disjoint. These restrictions genuinely 'rule out tractability in the parameterized setting' as claimed.

The positive results avoid the standard leaf-to-root dynamic programming paradigm, which the authors convincingly argue is incompatible with the problem. The two-step approach (structural normalization of the SCM followed by a fixed-parameter sized LP, Theorem 5; the 'single hidden variable determines the structural function' construction in Lemma 10 for Theorem 11) is a genuinely different technique for treewidth-based tractability and could plausibly find further applications, as the authors suggest.

The treatment of definitions is careful and honest: the deviation from prior SAT* definitions (sets of inequalities rather than arbitrary Boolean combinations) is explicitly flagged and justified via Theorem 1; the extension to marginalization operators is honestly bounded (EXPTIME membership vs. NEXP-completeness, so no lift), and the constant-nesting-depth workaround is correctly identified.

Proofs are written out in full in the main text, including a worked example (Example 6) tracing the LP construction and the corresponding model; this aids verification and reproducibility of the mathematical arguments.
weaknesses: The practical significance of the 'gateways to tractability' is limited. The FPT algorithm of Theorem 5 runs in d^f(tw)*|ϕ|^O(1), and Theorem 11 runs in n!*(|ϕ|^O(1) + d^O(d^n)), which involves a double-exponential dependence on n in the exponent. Even the LP in Theorem 11 has up to d^(d^n) variables. For realistic causal models these running times are astronomically large, so the contribution is almost purely complexity-theoretic; the paper would benefit from a franker discussion of the gap between parameterized tractability and practical applicability.

The claim that the treewidth-based technique (Results 1 and 2) is 'entirely novel' is somewhat overstated. The core of Theorem 5—representing a consistent joint distribution via an LP over bags of a tree decomposition with marginalization consistency constraints—is structurally close to classical junction-tree/cluster-based consistency formulations and to LP-based approaches to probabilistic satisfiability going back to Nilsson [32] and Georgakopoulos et al. [20]; the novelty lies mainly in the reverse direction of the proof (constructing an SCM from an LP solution via chained hidden variables) rather than in the LP formulation itself.

The parameterization by d + n for the deeper layers (Result 5) feels weak: the algorithm enumerates all n! variable orders and the hardness results (Theorems 7-9) show that neither parameter alone suffices, so the gateway is narrow. The paper itself concedes the open question of even an XP algorithm for SATcounterfact_lin parameterized by n alone, which indicates the classification is less complete than the framing 'almost complete picture' suggests.

There is an asymmetry in the lower-bound strength: Results (3) and (6) are supported by W[1]-hardness (Theorem 8), but Result (4) for the lin-causal case and Result (5)'s tightness rely on NP-completeness statements (Theorems 9 and 7) whose relationship to FPT/XP in the parameterized sense is only argued indirectly (e.g., tw(ϕ) ≤ n in the discussion after Theorem 8). A cleaner separation of which hardness assumption rules out which algorithmic guarantee would improve rigor of the 'matching' claims.

The restriction to recursive SCMs with a fixed well-order ≺ and to single-variable, finite-domain hidden variables is silently load-bearing in several proofs (e.g., Lemma 10's partition argument and Observation 4's contraction procedure). The paper states the reduction from continuous exogenous domains to finite ones via [46], but does not discuss whether restricting to recursive models (as opposed to general SCMs, e.g., with cyclic or simultaneous structure) matches the definitions used in the works from which the hardness baselines are imported.

The paper contains no empirical component whatsoever—no implementation, no experiments, not even a discussion of whether the LP-based algorithms could be implemented and scaled on small instances. For a theory paper this is acceptable, but combined with the enormous running times it makes the contribution relevant to a rather specialized audience even within the ICML community.

Minor presentation issues: the running-time claim in Theorem 5's proof (d^f(tw)|ϕ|^O(1)) is stated with an unspecified f and the XP/FPT dichotomy within the single algorithm is left implicit; the proof of Theorem 5 implicitly assumes connectivity handling for disconnected primal graphs is routine without spelling it out; and the phrase 'dashing any hope' is informal for a paper of this register.
